title: 14 · Dispute card, chargeback și fraude > 7. Fluxul emitentului > 7.1 Diagrama

section: 7.2 Pachetul de probe (inferență din regulile Visa, cazurile CSALB, formularul BCR și art. 171)

text:
1. **Tranzacția:** datele tranzacției, procesării și debitării; sumă, monedă, ARN; canal, POS entry mode, token sau wallet.
2. **3DS / Visa Secure:** ECI, CAVV, versiune 3DS, Authentication Confirmation, ora autentificării.
3. **Aprobarea din Smart Mobile:** metodă (biometrie sau PIN), dispozitiv, oră, suma și comerciantul afișate (DSP-10), versiunea fluxului.
4. **Dispozitive:** istoricul legărilor, IP, dispozitive noi, semnale de acces la distanță, sesiuni neobișnuite, transferuri fracționate sub limite (DSP-50).
5. **Cardul:** cronologia stării (pierdut sau furat raportat la …, blocat, reemis).
6. **Comerciantul:** MCC, țară, SEE sau nu (în afara SEE, SCA poate lipsi).
7. **Istoricul băncii:** fraudele raportate (CE3.0) și disputele din 120 de zile (limita de 35).
8. **Incidentele tehnice** din ziua tranzacției (art. 171).
9. **Plângerea la poliție,** dacă există; nu condiționează D+1 (DSP-54).
10. **Narativul clientului,** ca date neîncrezute.
11. **Pentru 13.x:** dovada contactării comerciantului, a anulării sau returului, datele de livrare, plata prin alt mijloc (lista din formularul BCR [P], ca proxy).

**Ce nu știm:** volumele absolute Raiffeisen (reclamații, dispute), împărțirea pe fraudă / dispută de consum / eroare, timpii de soluționare, rata de câștig la chargeback, FTE, backlog; formularul de dispută, politica de credit provizoriu, comisionul pentru dispută nejustificată, cerința de plângere la poliție. text:
Fake courier SMS with a payment link (SMS fals de la curier cu link de plată)
Family: smishing. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: transfer, card.
The customer receives an SMS (sometimes a WhatsApp message) in the name of a courier or the postal service saying a parcel could not be delivered and a small fee must be paid; a DNSC alert from May 2026 cites a 3.57 lei fee to reschedule delivery, in the name of DHL, and an alert from January 2025 had the fake page ask for the fee to be paid through Revolut. The link opens a near-perfect copy of the courier site on a different domain, which asks for the full card details and then for the one-time code the bank sends by SMS. The attacker is online while the victim types: the card data is submitted to a merchant, the bank's code reaches the victim, the code typed on the fake page is used at once, and if it expires the page asks for another one. The customer thinks they paid a few lei and later finds an unknown card payment, or a transfer when the lure is turned into a fake bank login.
Steps: 1) Customer receives an unsolicited SMS in the name of a courier or the post: delivery failed, pay a small fee or confirm the address. 2) The link opens a lookalike page whose domain is not the courier's; the form looks professional. 3) The page asks for the full card number, expiry, CVV and then the SMS one-time code from the bank. 4) The attacker, connected in real time, runs a payment with those data and relays the code the victim types; if the code expires the page requests a new one. 5) The payment goes through at a merchant the customer does not know; the customer notices a bank SMS or notification and calls the bank, usually minutes to hours later.
Bank signals: Several 3-D Secure SMS OTP challenges for the same card within minutes (the fake page asks for a new code when the first one expires).; Card-not-present authorisation completed seconds after the OTP was entered, with the OTP delivered to the customer's own registered phone.; Payment authenticated with an SMS OTP at a merchant the customer has never used, so it looks customer-authenticated (ECI 05, CAVV present).; Merchant outside Romania or the EEA whose descriptor has nothing to do with a courier or the post.; No banking-app login around the time of the payment (card flow only), unlike the credential-theft variant.; Payment still pending or unsettled when the customer reports it, typically minutes to hours after the click.
Sources: Tentativă de fraudă online care folosește imaginea unei companii de curierat. text:
Phishing link to a fake bank login page (Link de phishing către o pagină falsă de autentificare a băncii)
Family: phishing. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: transfer, transfer_instant.
A message (SMS, e-mail, WhatsApp or social-media DM) in the bank's name says the account is blocked, the data must be updated or a payment must be unblocked. The link opens a copy of the bank's login page on another domain; a padlock or https does not prove legitimacy. The customer types the username and password and the SMS code, or approves a push request, believing it is the bank's own check. The attacker, working in real time, logs in to the genuine banking service, often enrols a new device with the stolen data, adds a new payee and sends one or more transfers, instant when available. The pattern is the one described in the CJEU C-70/25 case (a fake buyer's link to a bank-lookalike site, credentials typed, transfer made) as summarised in docs/context/14.
Steps: 1) Customer receives a message in the bank's name (blocked account, data update, unblock a payment) with a link. 2) The link opens a lookalike login page on a domain that is not the bank's. 3) Customer enters credentials and the SMS code, or approves the push request the page triggers. 4) Attacker logs in to the real service, enrols a new device or session and adds a new payee. 5) One or more transfers leave the account, often most of the balance; the customer sees a notification or loses access and calls the bank.
Bank signals: New device enrolled (via SMS OTP or web login) minutes after a login from an unfamiliar IP, geography or user agent.; SCA for the enrolment or the payment is satisfied on the NEW device; the customer's usual device shows no approval at that time.; New payee created within minutes of the enrolment, followed by one or more transfers (instant when available), often most of the available balance.; OTP text or approval screen shows an amount and payee the customer did not intend, or an OTP issued for login or enrolment is reused to authorise a payment.; Short gap (minutes, not days) between the first anomalous login and the first payment.; Attempts to raise limits or move savings immediately after the first transfer.

text:
Marketplace fake buyer sends a payment or courier link (Fals cumpărător pe un site de anunțuri trimite un link de plată sau de curierat)
Family: marketplace. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: card_visa_secure. Channels: card, transfer.
A seller lists an item on a classifieds site such as OLX, Publi24 or Lajumate. A buyer replies, says the money is already paid or will be paid at once, and moves the chat to WhatsApp. He sends a link to collect the money or to arrange a courier. The page, which imitates the platform, a courier or the bank, asks for card data, the card PIN or CVV, the static and dynamic 3-D Secure passwords, or online-banking credentials, always on the pretext that this is how the seller receives money. The data are then used for card payments, often at foreign merchants, or for transfers. In a CSALB case the seller of concert tickets typed a 3-D Secure code on a fake bank interface and two payments of 4,902 lei each followed, and the bank refused a refund because of the 3-D Secure authorisation. A mirror variant uses fake listings at very low prices to send buyers to a card-data phishing page.
Steps: 1) Seller posts an item; a buyer answers quickly, claims to have paid, and asks to continue on WhatsApp. 2) Buyer sends a link to receive the payment or to use a courier service. 3) The page asks for card number, expiry, CVV, PIN or the 3-D Secure passwords, or for online-banking credentials. 4) A caller posing as the platform's or shop's operator may phone for the SMS codes as a bank verification. 5) Instead of money arriving, one or more payments leave the card or account; the seller finds out when the expected credit does not appear.
Bank signals: Card payments authenticated with a 3-D Secure code typed by the customer on a third-party page (ECI 05, CAVV present), so the bank can claim customer authentication.; Two or more card payments of the same amount within minutes at a foreign or first-time merchant (CSALB case: two payments of 4,902 lei).; Payments unsettled or pending for days when the customer reports them (CSALB case: three days).; Customer expected an incoming credit from the sale; the account shows only outgoing debits around the listing date.; In the transfer variant: login from a new device or IP right after the customer shared credentials, then a new payee and an outgoing transfer.; Phone contact from a caller who obtained SMS codes: OTP requests clustered in time with no matching customer action.
Sources: Cele mai frecvente tipuri de fraudă din România · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2021-10 [P]; 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]; În siguranță online (Raiffeisen Bank România, security guidance) · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-10 [P]

text:
Fake bank security call: approve it in the app to stop the fraud (Apel fals de la „securitatea băncii”: aprobă în aplicație ca să oprești frauda)
Family: vishing. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: vishing_securitate. Channels: transfer, card.
A caller whose number is spoofed to look like the bank's, or very similar, says he is from the bank's security or fraud department. The pretext is a suspicious transaction, an attempt to steal the customer's money, or a loan the customer supposedly requested and that was approved; the customer is told to react at once. To stop or cancel it, the customer is asked to confirm an operation in the banking app, read out the SMS codes, give personal and banking details or install an application. The customer approves a push request or enters the code, believing it cancels the fraud, but it authorises a payment, a new device or a limit change. Sometimes a second caller, posing as police, confirms the first. Police, ARB and DNSC describe this as a current campaign, and the CSALB case files show banks treating the in-app approval as proof of authorisation.
Steps: 1) A call arrives from a spoofed number that looks like the bank's; the caller already knows basic data about the customer. 2) He claims a fraud attempt or a loan approved in the customer's name and creates urgency. 3) The customer is told to confirm or cancel the operation in the app, read SMS codes or install an app. 4) The customer approves the push or enters the code; the operation executed is a payment, a new payee, a new device or a loan. 5) The caller may hand the customer over to a second 'official' (police, central bank) who confirms the story. 6) The customer hangs up, calls the real bank and learns that no one from the bank called.
Bank signals: Payment, new payee, new device or limit change approved in the app from the customer's own enrolled device (no unfamiliar device or IP).; Approval screen shows the real amount and payee but the customer approved anyway (screen_showed_amount_and_payee true), or the OTP text names a different purpose.; New payee created minutes before the payment, then an immediate transfer of a large part of the balance.; Sequence login, add payee, approve, transfer completed in a few minutes while the customer is on a call (the call itself is invisible to the bank).; A consumer or overdraft loan taken in the app shortly before outgoing transfers (the 'loan approved' pretext).; No outbound customer call to the bank before the payment; the customer contacts the bank only afterwards.
Sources: Poliția Română, Directoratul Național de Securitate Cibernetică și Asociația Română a Băncilor avertizează asupra riscului de fraudă prin apeluri telefonice false (spoofed) · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2024-05 [P]; Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2025-10 [P]; În siguranță online (Raiffeisen Bank România, security guidance) · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-10 [P]; 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]; Comunicat de presă – Directoratul Național de Securitate Cibernetică (ING SAFE Talks, 14.07.2026) · AGERPRES (DNSC communiqué) · 2026-07 [P]

text:
Transfer to a 'safe' or 'custody' account (Transfer într-un cont „sigur” sau „în custodie”)
Family: app_scam. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer_instant, transfer.
A spoofed caller presents as a bank officer, then as a police officer and as a representative of the central bank, and says the customer's savings are at risk or evidence must be protected. The customer is told to move the money immediately to a 'safe account' or to intermediate accounts where it will be held 'in custody' during the investigation. The customer, under constant time pressure, makes one or more transfers, often instant, to accounts dictated by the caller. The receiving accounts are emptied quickly, the money is dispersed across other accounts or converted to crypto, and the same victim may be approached again with a new pretext.
Steps: 1) Spoofed call from the 'bank', handed over to a 'police officer' and a 'central bank representative' who confirm that the account is compromised. 2) The customer is told to protect the savings by moving them to a safe account or custody account given by the caller. 3) The customer logs in and makes the transfers, often instant, to the accounts dictated; the caller stays on the line. 4) The recipients forward the money within minutes to other accounts, cash or crypto. 5) The customer realises the story is false when the caller disappears or the real bank says nobody called.
Bank signals: Instant transfer or several transfers to new payees (created minutes earlier) approved from the customer's own device.; Payee names are private persons or unrelated companies, never the bank, the police or the central bank named in the story.; Transferred amount is a large share of the balance or of savings, well above the customer's usual transfers.; Receiving accounts forward the funds out within minutes to other accounts, cash or crypto (mule-like pass-through, relevant for AML referral).; Several transfers in quick succession, sometimes to different payees, during a period that matches an inbound call.; Receiving accounts at other banks or payment institutions; the same account receiving from several unrelated senders in a short time.
Sources: Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2025-10 [P]; Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB și Mastercard lansează campania națională „Uniți împotriva escrocheriilor” · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2026-03 [P]; În siguranță online (Raiffeisen Bank România, security guidance) · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-10 [P]; 2025 Report on Payment Fraud (EBA/REP/2025/40) · EBA and ECB · 2025-12 [P]

text:
Fake bank, police and central bank callers: take a loan and feed a crypto ATM (Apelanți falși de la bancă, poliție și BNR: iei un credit și depui banii la un bancomat de criptomonede)
Family: impersonation_authority. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: vishing_securitate. Channels: transfer.
Callers appear in turn as a bank employee, a police officer and a representative of the central bank (BNR) or of criminal investigators, and tell the customer that his or her identity or banking data are being used fraudulently. The customer is walked through taking out a personal loan, often around 70,000 to 110,000 lei, withdrawing the money in cash and depositing it at a crypto (Bitcoin) ATM, using QR codes and sometimes repeated deposits of 10,000 lei. The callers stay on the phone while the customer is at the bank or the ATM, and may ask the customer to confirm the operations by calling two given numbers. The customer is left with a loan to repay and a cash-to-crypto conversion that cannot be recovered; banks tell CSALB that the case is under police investigation and that the customer let the criminals in.
Steps: 1) A spoofed call arrives; the caller says he is from the bank, then 'police', then 'central bank', and claims the customer's identity or accounts are being used for fraud. 2) The customer is told to take a personal loan, supposedly to protect or recover the money. 3) The customer withdraws the loan proceeds in cash, at the counter or ATM, while the caller stays on the line. 4) The cash is deposited at a crypto ATM in repeated amounts (for example 10,000 lei) against QR codes the caller supplies. 5) The customer is asked to 'approve' the operations by calling given numbers; later the callers vanish and the customer is left with the loan.
Bank signals: Personal loan disbursed shortly after the calls begin, for a customer with no comparable borrowing history; the instalment can exceed 30% of net income (CSALB case: 1,450 lei per month).; Large cash withdrawals, in round amounts, within hours or days of the disbursement, at the counter or at ATMs.; Repeated round-sum cash movements (for example 10,000 lei, 14 deposits in one case) that match deposits at a crypto ATM outside the bank's perimeter.; Staff at the counter or branch can observe the customer on the phone with a third party while transacting.; Loan proceeds do not remain in the account: balance returns to its pre-loan level within the same day or week.; After the event: the customer asks for suspension of instalments and for no Credit Bureau reporting, citing a police complaint.
Sources: Banking Loan Fraud Cases on the Rise: Dozens of Cases Reported Each Month by Consumers to CSALB · CSALB · 2026-09 [P]; Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB și Mastercard lansează campania națională „Uniți împotriva escrocheriilor” · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2026-03 [P]; Emotional Manipulation, Increasingly Used in Fraud Attempts Targeting Romanians' Bank Accounts · CSALB · 2025-05 [P]; Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2025-10 [P]

text:
Fake investment platform promoted by deepfake or celebrity ads (Platformă falsă de investiții promovată prin reclame deepfake sau cu persoane publice)
Family: investment. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: card, transfer.
Social-media ads promise fast, safe returns, often using the image and voice of a public figure, including AI-made deepfake videos (the central bank warned in February 2026 about videos using its Governor's image to push investments on a non-existent platform, and a press report of a later warning names a fake app called Profit Gold Românesc), or imitating listed companies such as Hidroelectrica, Transgaz and Transelectrica. The customer leaves contact details in a form, and call-centre 'consultants' phone repeatedly from Romanian or UK numbers. The first investment is small, a few hundred euro, paid by card or by buying crypto sent to wallets the scammers name; the platform shows growing profits and the customer is asked to invest more, sometimes tens of thousands of euro, and to install a remote-access app such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer 'for support'. Withdrawals are blocked with invented fees, taxes or guarantees, and loans may be opened in the customer's name through the banking app. After the loss, fake 'recovery' services or lawyers ask a fee to get the money back.
Steps: 1) Customer sees an ad (a public figure, a deepfake or a listed company's name) promising quick, safe gains and fills in a contact form. 2) Call-centre 'consultants' call repeatedly, from Romanian or UK numbers, and guide the first small deposit by card or crypto purchase. 3) A fake platform shows profits; the customer is pushed to invest more and to install AnyDesk or TeamViewer. 4) Larger transfers follow, sometimes funded by a loan; the scammers may use the remote access to move money or open accounts. 5) A withdrawal request triggers demands for fees, taxes or guarantees; contact then stops. 6) Fake recovery services appear and ask a commission to retrieve the money.
Bank signals: First payments to crypto exchanges, payment processors or foreign accounts start small (a few hundred euro) and escalate over days or weeks.; Card payments and transfers approved with SCA from the customer's own device, so the SCA evidence favours the bank.; In the remote-access variant: change of the phone number that receives authorisation codes, loan applications in the app, deposit closures, then transfers (CSALB).; Transactions continue after the customer asked the bank to block the account (CSALB case: RON 10,600 taken despite blocked accounts, then a 67,000 lei loan over 60 months through the mobile app).; Repeated payments to the same beneficiary or wallet that are described as fees or taxes to unlock a withdrawal.; Remote-control or screen-sharing tool detected on the device, if the app collects that telemetry.; Beneficiary accounts abroad or at payment institutions; after the loss, contact with the bank is often delayed because of shame.

text:
Romance scam leading to money requests or crypto 'investments' (Înșelăciune romantică ce duce la cereri de bani sau „investiții” în criptomonede)
Family: romance. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer, card.
The scammer builds a false emotional relationship with the customer on a dating or social-media platform, using a polished or stolen photo and insisting on text and calls only. After weeks of daily contact he or she invents an emergency such as a hospitalisation, an accident or financial trouble and asks for money, or introduces a crypto trading platform and persuades the customer to invest together. Police have seen romance and trading scams intertwined, and Europol describes criminals slowly building trust before convincing victims to put their savings into fraudulent crypto platforms. The customer sends several transfers or card payments, often to foreign accounts or exchanges, and only realises the scam when a withdrawal fails or the contact disappears. Victims are often ashamed and report late.
Steps: 1) Contact on a dating or social platform; the profile looks too perfect and the person avoids meeting or video calls. 2) Daily messages build trust and emotional dependence over weeks. 3) An emergency is invented (hospital, accident, financial problem), or a crypto platform is proposed as a joint investment. 4) The customer sends repeated transfers or card payments, often to different accounts and to crypto exchanges. 5) Fees are demanded to release money, or the contact vanishes; the customer reports late.
Bank signals: Repeated transfers over weeks to the same new foreign payee, or to several accounts, with rising amounts.; First-time payments to crypto exchanges or payment processors after the relationship began.; Payments approved with SCA from the customer's own device; the customer often overrides or ignores warning prompts.; Beneficiaries in different countries or payment institutions; descriptions that mention gifts, help, medical or travel costs.; Customer visits to the branch or calls asking to speed up or raise limits on transfers.

text:
WhatsApp message from a 'relative' with a broken phone and a new number (Mesaj WhatsApp de la o „rudă” cu telefonul stricat și număr nou)
Family: family_emergency. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer_instant, transfer.
The customer receives a written message, mostly on WhatsApp, from an unknown number: the sender claims to be a son, daughter or other relative whose phone is broken, gives a new number, and soon says he cannot use his banking app and needs an urgent bill paid. The customer is pressured to send money to the account of a 'friend'. Only written messages are used so the voice cannot be checked. The transfer is usually instant to an account in a third person's name; afterwards the real relative, called on the old number, knows nothing. The national campaign launched in March 2026 targets people aged 60 and over and recommends a 'family password' built from shared memories.
Steps: 1) A message arrives from an unknown number: 'hi, it is me, my phone broke, this is my new number'. 2) After a short exchange the sender says he cannot reach his banking app and asks the customer to pay an urgent bill or help a friend. 3) The customer receives an IBAN in a third person's name and sends an instant transfer. 4) A second request may follow within hours or the next day. 5) The customer calls the real relative on the old number and learns it was a scam.
Bank signals: First-time payee with a personal name that does not match the relative named in the story; instant transfer outside the customer's usual pattern.; Small-to-medium amount (CSALB 2025 WhatsApp-impersonation case: 3,500 lei), often with a description such as an urgent invoice or a loan.; Transfer approved with SCA from the customer's own device; no device or IP anomaly.; A second transfer to the same or another new payee within hours or the next day.; The receiving account collects instant transfers from several unrelated senders in a short time and forwards them out quickly (AML referral signal).; Customer profile skews to older customers in the campaign description; the bank cannot see the WhatsApp conversation.
Sources: Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB și Mastercard lansează campania națională „Uniți împotriva escrocheriilor” · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2026-03 [P]; 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]; Prevenirea fraudelor prin aplicații de mesagerie · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2025-05 [P]

text:
Cloned-voice call from a 'relative' in an accident or legal trouble (Apel cu voce clonată a unei „rude” aflate într-un accident sau în necaz)
Family: family_emergency. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer_instant, card.
The customer, often an older person, receives a phone call with an AI-cloned voice of a family member who claims to have had a serious accident or to be in legal trouble (the 'accident' scenario), or the voice of a grandchild who says he has been robbed and needs money at once (the 'grandchild in distress' scenario). The customer is pressed to send money urgently. In a CSALB case the caller, impersonating the victim's son, obtained a photo of the card and the 3-D Secure approval, and the bank refused a refund because the payment had been authorised. The national campaign recommends agreeing a family password to verify callers.
Steps: 1) Phone call: a voice that sounds like the relative reports an accident, an arrest or a robbery and asks for money immediately. 2) The caller discourages checking and keeps the customer on the line. 3) The customer makes an urgent transfer, or gives the card details and approves a 3-D Secure request in the app. 4) The real relative is reached later and knows nothing; the customer reports the loss.
Bank signals: 3-D Secure or in-app approval of a card payment or an instant transfer while the customer is on a call, from the customer's own device.; Card details given by phone: the payment is card-not-present and authenticated, so ECI 05 and CAVV are present (CSALB case: 5,000 lei, bank refused citing authorisation).; First-time payee or merchant, round amount, outside the customer's usual pattern.; Short time between the start of the unusual activity and the payment (minutes).; Customer profile is typically an older person; no device or IP anomaly.

text:
WhatsApp account hijack through a fake 'vote' link, then loan requests to contacts (Preluarea contului WhatsApp printr-un link fals de „vot”, apoi cereri de bani către contacte)
Family: account_takeover. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer_instant, transfer.
The customer receives a Romanian-language message from a known contact asking for a vote for a girl in a contest whose prize is a scholarship in France. The link opens a page that looks like the messaging app and tells the user to open the app and enter a code. The attackers have already asked the service to link the victim's number to their own device, so the app on the victim's phone expects an eight-character code, and typing it authorises the attackers' device. The attackers then write to the victim's contacts asking for urgent loans or transfers, usually to bank accounts that are not in the requester's name, and re-send the vote lure to spread the scam. For the bank, the paying customer is a contact of the hijacked account, who sends an instant transfer to a person the request never named.
Steps: 1) A contact's already hijacked account sends the 'please vote for her' message with a link. 2) The link opens a fake page that looks like the messaging app and tells the user to open the app and enter a code. 3) The code is the pairing code the attackers requested for that number; entering it links the attackers' device to the account. 4) The attackers message the account's contacts asking for an urgent loan or payment to a third-party account, and re-send the vote lure. 5) A contact sends an instant transfer; later the real owner says the account was hacked.
Bank signals: Instant transfer or transfer to a new payee whose name does not match the person who asked for the money on WhatsApp.; Small-to-medium amount described as a loan or urgent help, approved from the paying customer's own device.; Several senders paying the same account within hours, because the lure spreads through the hijacked contact list (AML referral signal).; Receiving account at another bank or payment institution that forwards funds out quickly.; A different customer (the hijacked owner) reports the takeover; there is no bank-side compromise on either account.

text:
Remote-access app installed at a scammer's request, then the banking app is operated from outside (Aplicație de acces la distanță instalată la cererea escrocului, apoi aplicația bancară este folosită de la distanță)
Family: remote_access. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: vishing_securitate. Channels: transfer, transfer_instant, card.
Under the pretext of investment support, a fraud check by the 'bank', a tax or health-contribution refund, or technical help, the customer or a company representative is persuaded to install a remote-control application such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer, or to share the screen. The attacker then operates the customer's banking app or browser session: he can see balances, apply for loans, close deposits, initiate payments, change passwords and change the phone number that receives authorisation codes. In a business variant warned about by ARB in March 2026, callers posing as ANAF, CNAS or banks offer VAT or health-contribution refunds or announce alleged debts, and ask for screen sharing, banking credentials or transfers to given accounts. Because the payments come from the customer's genuine device and session, banks usually treat them as authorised, while customers say they never approved the transfers.
Steps: 1) A call or message offers help with an 'investment', a 'fraud check', a refund or a debt, and asks the customer to install a remote-control app or to share the screen. 2) The customer installs the app and reads out the connection code; the attacker sees and controls the device. 3) The attacker opens the banking app or session, views balances and may apply for a loan or close a deposit. 4) The attacker changes the phone number or password used for authorisation and initiates transfers, often in several steps. 5) The customer notices money gone, uninstalls the app and calls the bank; transfers may continue after the block request.
Bank signals: Payments from the customer's genuine enrolled device and usual IP, but with an abnormal rhythm: rapid navigation, new payee, amount well above usual.; Change of the phone number or password used for authorisation shortly before the transfers (CSALB: attackers could change the number that receives the codes).; Loan applied for in the app, or a deposit closed, followed by outgoing transfers (CSALB: attackers can apply for loans and close deposits).; Successive transfers staying under the security limits (CSALB 2026 case: RON 90,000 taken in successive transactions to circumvent limits).; Transfers continue after the customer asked the bank to block access (CSALB 2025 case).; Remote-control or screen-sharing tool installed or running, if the app collects device telemetry.; Business variant: a company's internet-banking user is given away and payments go to accounts dictated by the caller, often before the company notices.

sources.title: Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing
Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit
10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB

text:
SIM swap to intercept SMS codes (SIM swap pentru interceptarea codurilor SMS)
Family: account_takeover. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: sim_swap. Channels: transfer, card.
Criminals who already hold some of the victim's data persuade the mobile operator, through social engineering or forged documents, to move the victim's number onto a SIM card they control. The victim's phone loses signal while the attackers receive every call and SMS, including the bank's one-time codes and password-reset messages. With them they take over online banking or card tokens, add a payee and make transfers or purchases before the customer can get the line back. Police list SIM swap among the technical manoeuvres that accompany spoofed-call schemes, and Europol notes that it is used to obtain the OTP that authorises transfers but that cases fell in 2022, probably because operators tightened customer identification.
Steps: 1) Attackers collect personal data through phishing, vishing or leaks. 2) They contact the mobile operator (or an agent) and obtain a replacement SIM or a number transfer. 3) The victim's phone loses service while the attackers' SIM receives SMS and calls. 4) Using the OTPs, they reset credentials or enrol a device in the banking app, add a payee and move money. 5) The customer notices the lost signal or the bank notifications, contacts the operator and the bank, often hours later.
Bank signals: SIM replacement or number-port event at the operator (sim_events) in the hours before the first anomalous action, where the bank receives such data.; OTP SMS delivered to a SIM that changed shortly before; sudden loss of the customer's usual mobile signal reported by the customer.; Password reset or device enrolment completed with an SMS OTP immediately after the SIM event.; Phone number registered in the bank profile changed (CSALB 2025 case: home-banking access lost after the number was changed).; New payee and one or more transfers within hours, from the new device.; Customer contacts the bank from another phone number, and the first contact comes after the money has left.
Sources: Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2025-10 [P]; Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]; 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]

meta.name_ro: Malware Android instalat dintr-un link, apoi aplicația bancară este folosită abuziv

sources.title: Banking Loan Fraud Cases on the Rise: Dozens of Cases Reported Each Month by Consumers to CSALB
Raport asupra stabilității financiare, decembrie 2025
DNSC avertizează asupra unei amenințări cibernetice ce vizează utilizatorii de Android (Rafel RAT)

text:
Android malware installed from a link, then the banking app is abused (Malware Android instalat dintr-un link, apoi aplicația bancară este folosită abuziv)
Family: account_takeover. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: transfer, transfer_instant.
The victim is lured, through a link in an SMS or a WhatsApp message, a fake update or a look-alike app, into installing a malicious Android application. The application works as a remote-access tool or banking trojan: it can read SMS, see the screen, run in the background and let the attackers operate the phone. In a CSALB case the malware arrived through an application installed via WhatsApp; the criminals opened an online bank account in the victim's name, took a loan of 29,000 lei and stole 90,000 lei in successive transactions that stayed below security limits, half of it from an account where the victim was an authorised representative for other people. The bank answered that the payments had been authenticated in the home-banking app with the security code or biometrics and executed according to the IBAN given. DNSC warned in 2024 about the Rafel RAT, spread through fake apps, mails, SMS and social media.
Steps: 1) Victim receives a link (SMS, WhatsApp, e-mail or social media) that leads to a malicious app or a fake update. 2) The app asks for broad permissions and installs; it hides and may read SMS and control the screen. 3) Attackers connect to the device, sometimes for hours, and operate the banking app or open an online account and loan in the victim's name. 4) Funds are moved in several successive transactions, often staying under security limits, to other accounts. 5) The victim notices a loan notice, an SMS or empty accounts and reports the loss to the bank and the police.
Bank signals: SCA satisfied with the app security code or biometrics on the customer's enrolled device, so the bank sees valid authentication (stated in the bank's reply in the CSALB case).; Online account opened and loan applied for in the customer's name shortly before the transfers (CSALB case).; Funds withdrawn in a series of successive transactions designed to stay under security limits (CSALB case).; Transfers between the customer's own accounts first, then out, including from an account where the customer is only an authorised representative.; Device with an outdated operating system or integrity flags; in the DNSC Rafel RAT warning, 87.5% of the devices involved ran Android versions that no longer received security updates.; Sessions at unusual hours or lasting hours, with abnormal speed; no new-device enrolment because the customer's own phone is used.
Sources: Banking Loan Fraud Cases on the Rise: Dozens of Cases Reported Each Month by Consumers to CSALB · CSALB · 2026-09 [P]; Raport asupra stabilității financiare, decembrie 2025 · Banca Națională a României · 2025-12 [P]; DNSC avertizează asupra unei amenințări cibernetice ce vizează utilizatorii de Android (Rafel RAT) · AGERPRES (DNSC warning) · 2024-07 [S]

meta.name_ro: Credit sau card de credit luat pe numele victimei (furt de identitate, identificare video, acces în aplicație)

sources.title: Banking Loan Fraud Cases on the Rise: Dozens of Cases Reported Each Month by Consumers to CSALB
10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB

text:
Loan or credit card taken in the victim's name (identity theft, video identification, app access) (Credit sau card de credit luat pe numele victimei (furt de identitate, identificare video, acces în aplicație))
Family: account_takeover. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: transfer.
Using stolen credentials, remote access to a phone, or an identity-verification video that the victim recorded for a fake 'investment broker' on social media, criminals open an online account or apply for a personal loan or credit card in the victim's name. The proceeds are moved at once to external accounts, crypto platforms or cash. The victim learns of the debt from the loan notification or the first instalment and asks the bank to cancel the loan, to suspend the instalments and not to report delays to the Credit Bureau. The central bank's representative in CSALB warns that video-identification recordings can be reused for deepfakes. In the cases CSALB listed in 2026, banks had closed or rejected every request, often because the police were investigating and the customer had given the criminals access.
Steps: 1) The victim gives away credentials, phone access or a recorded identification video (for example to a fake broker or investment app). 2) The criminals complete onboarding or a loan application in the victim's name, in the app or online. 3) The loan is disbursed and quickly transferred to external accounts or turned into cash or crypto. 4) The victim sees the loan notice or the first instalment, reports to the bank and the police and disputes the contract. 5) The bank refuses, arguing the customer's own authentication or access.
Bank signals: Online account opening or loan origination completed with remote or video identification, followed within hours by outgoing transfers of the proceeds to external accounts.; Loan amounts in the documented cases range from 29,000 to 110,000 lei, at or near the customer's maximum; a 60-month loan was taken through the mobile app despite the customer having blocked the accounts.; Contact details (phone, e-mail) at origination differ from those on file, or are changed right after.; New device enrolled at origination; no borrowing history; instalment above 30% of net income in at least one case.; Identification session performed shortly after the customer interacted with a third party (the 'broker'); the video could have been reused.; After the event: police complaint reference, request to suspend instalments and not to report to the Credit Bureau.
Sources: Banking Loan Fraud Cases on the Rise: Dozens of Cases Reported Each Month by Consumers to CSALB · CSALB · 2026-09 [P]; 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]

sources.title: 2025 Report on Payment Fraud (EBA/REP/2025/40)

Raport Anual 2025, p. 41
Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit
Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB și Mastercard lansează campania națională „Uniți împotriva escrocheriilor”

text:
Stolen card details used for card-not-present purchases (Datele cardului furate și folosite pentru plăți online fără card fizic)
Family: card_not_present. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: card_ecom_fara_3ds. Channels: card.
Card details (number, expiry, CVV) are obtained through phishing, a data breach, an infostealer or digital skimming of an online shop's checkout page, and are sold on card-dump sites. Fraudsters use them for online purchases, typically at merchants that do not apply strong customer authentication or that are outside the EEA. The EBA/ECB report for 2024 finds that remote card payments were about 83% of all card fraud, that in most card fraud the fraudster directly issues the payment order with stolen credentials, and that fraud rates were about seventeen times higher when the payee was outside the EEA. The customer sees an unknown online payment, often at a foreign website, without having received any code or approval request, and reports it while the payment may still be pending. Raiffeisen's 2025 annual report says about 64% of its registered complaints are contested card transactions.
Steps: 1) Card data are stolen by phishing, a breach, an infostealer or digital skimming of a checkout page and are sold on card-dump sites. 2) Fraudsters use the data at online merchants, typically ones that do not apply 3-D Secure or are outside the EEA. 3) Purchases go through without a code or approval request to the cardholder. 4) The customer sees a notification or a statement line for a merchant never used and blocks the card. 5) The customer disputes the payment; it may still be pending, and the bank may or may not be able to stop it.
Bank signals: E-commerce authorisation with no 3-D Secure (no CAVV, ECI 07) or under an SCA exemption, often at a merchant outside the EEA where SCA is not legally required.; First-time merchant and merchant country; merchant category unrelated to the customer's habits.; Several payments within minutes, sometimes at night.; No banking-app session or SCA event around the payment.; Payment still pending authorisation (not yet settled) when the customer reports it.; Card-present activity of the real card elsewhere in the same period.
Sources: 2025 Report on Payment Fraud (EBA/REP/2025/40) · EBA and ECB · 2025-12 [P]; Joint EBA-ECB report on payment fraud: strong authentication remains effective but fraudsters are adapting · ECB · 2025-12 [P]; Raport Anual 2025, p. 41 · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-04 [P]; Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]; Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB și Mastercard lansează campania națională „Uniți împotriva escrocheriilor” · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2026-03 [P]

meta.name_ro: Testarea cardurilor de către boți înaintea unor achiziții mai mari

sources.title: Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit

text:
Card testing by bots before larger purchases (Testarea cardurilor de către boți înaintea unor achiziții mai mari)
Family: card_not_present. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: card_ecom_fara_3ds. Channels: card.
Bots test whether stolen or generated card data are valid by sending many automated authorisation attempts to online merchants, often at the same time. Europol describes this carding as usually performed by bots that test the validity of stolen card data and then make purchases, with criminals running simultaneous automated operations to attempt purchase authorisation. The cardholder may see a few tiny or declined online charges at unknown sites, followed by a larger purchase, or only the decline notifications, and often has no idea how the details were obtained. No Romanian-specific source describing the pattern was found.
Steps: 1) Card details from a breach, skimmer or dump are loaded into a bot. 2) The bot fires many small authorisation attempts across merchants, often in parallel. 3) Cards that pass are used for larger purchases or sold on. 4) The cardholder sees tiny or declined charges, then a bigger one, and blocks the card.
Bank signals: Many authorisation attempts for the same card within seconds or minutes, at different merchants or from different IPs, run by automated clients.; A high share of declines for invalid CVV, expiry or card number.; Very small amounts first, then a larger purchase once a card is confirmed valid.; Attempts without 3-D Secure at merchants with weak controls; the same BIN range may be hit repeatedly.; The real card has no history at these merchants and there is no banking-app session.
Sources: Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]
title: Card testing by bots before larger purchases

meta.name_ro: Card înrolat într-un portofel digital pe dispozitivul fraudatorului

sources.title: 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB
Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit

text:
Card enrolled in a mobile wallet on the fraudster's device (Card înrolat într-un portofel digital pe dispozitivul fraudatorului)
Family: account_takeover. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: card_visa_secure. Channels: card.
The victim's card is added to a mobile wallet (Google Pay in the CSALB cases) on a device the criminals control. In one CSALB case the victim was manipulated into giving the card details and authorising the enrolment on a foreign device, and unauthorised wallet payments followed; in another, after a phone theft, the card enrolled on the stolen device was used for ten unauthorised transactions totalling 50,071 lei. Europol describes the technique: fraudsters obtain the OTP linked to tokenised cards and connect the stolen card data to existing mobile payment systems to buy goods or take cash. Token payments carry device-level authentication, so the bank often treats them as authenticated and the scheme chargeback route is weak.
Steps: 1) The criminals obtain the card details, by social engineering or from a stolen phone, and trigger the wallet enrolment. 2) The bank sends an enrolment OTP or approval request; the victim is tricked into giving or approving it, or the thief already holds the phone. 3) The card is tokenised on the criminals' device. 4) A burst of contactless or in-app payments follows, sometimes ten or more transactions. 5) The customer notices the notifications or the loss of the phone and reports the card.
Bank signals: Token provisioning event for a new device (a device PAN reference) shortly after an OTP or approval for enrolment.; Burst of token payments in a short window after provisioning (CSALB case: ten transactions, 50,071 lei in total).; Token device differs from the customer's enrolled devices; payment locations differ from the customer's usual location.; Payments authenticated at device level (token cryptogram, wallet unlock), so ECI and CAVV evidence favours the bank.; Customer reports a stolen phone or a recent call asking for card details and codes.
Sources: 10 Banking Fraud Methods and Channels: What Consumers Report to CSALB · CSALB · 2025-10 [P]; Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]
title: Card enrolled in a mobile wallet on the fraudster's device

text:
Fake parking fee, online fine or refund notice leading to a card-data page (Taxă de parcare, amendă online sau rambursare falsă care duce la o pagină de date de card)
Family: phishing. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: card.
Messages or pop-ups in the name of a public authority or a parking operator tell the customer there is an unpaid parking fee, an online fine or a refund. A DNSC alert reported on 27 July 2026 describes SMS messages about an unpaid parking fee and a 'last chance to pay without penalties' that open a fake page imitating official ones and asking for personal and banking data. Another DNSC alert, reported on 15 June 2026, describes pop-ups served by ad networks on websites announcing an 'online fine of 2,480 lei', using the name and logo of DNSC itself and redirecting to a page that asks for card details. Europol lists overpayments, tax requests and announcements of detected crimes among the usual phishing narratives. The card data typed in are used for card payments, with or without an OTP.
Steps: 1) Customer receives an SMS about an unpaid parking fee, or sees a pop-up announcing an online fine or a refund. 2) The link or pop-up leads to a page that imitates an official payment page and carries an institution's logo. 3) The page asks for personal data and the card number, expiry and CVV, and may ask for the SMS code. 4) The attackers use the data for card payments; the customer sees an unknown charge. 5) The customer calls the bank and files a report with the police.
Bank signals: Card-not-present payments at foreign or first-time merchants after the customer typed card data (and possibly an OTP) on a page branded as an authority.; OTP or 3-D Secure challenges that match no payment the customer intended, sometimes several in a row.; The lure amount (a parking fee, a 2,480 lei fine) does not match the disputed payment amounts.; No banking-app login; card flow only.; Customer reports within hours, while the payment may still be pending.
Sources: Atenție la SMS-urile cu taxe de parcare! sources.title: Au vrut să plătească parcarea, dar au rămas fără bani: șoferi din București și Constanța, victimele unei fraude cu coduri QR false
Poliția Capitalei: au fost depistate persoanele care au lipit pe panourile pentru plata parcării din Sectorul 1 stickere cu coduri QR diferite de cele originale

text:
Fake QR code stickers on parking payment panels (Autocolante cu coduri QR false pe panourile de plată a parcării)
Family: phishing. PSD2 class: unauthorized. Scenario: phishing_link. Channels: card.
In July 2025 fraudsters stuck fake QR codes over the genuine ones on parking payment panels in Bucharest and Constanța. Drivers who scanned them were redirected to cloned payment sites, typed their card details, and the payments went to unknown accounts. In Constanța the operator alerted the police on 24 July, at least one victim lost 700 lei, a criminal case for computer fraud was opened and the city temporarily suspended QR payment for parking; in Bucharest the municipal parking company found panels with QR stickers in a different colour. Bucharest police carried out five house searches on 6 November 2025 and found two suspects, one of whom is in jail in Belgium for similar offences, and investigators said the data was used to collect vehicle registration numbers and payment instrument details.
Steps: 1) Fraudsters stick a lookalike QR code over the real one on a parking payment panel. 2) A driver scans it to pay for parking and lands on a cloned payment site. 3) The site asks for card details; the data are captured and used for payments to unknown accounts. 4) The driver notices the charge or that the parking is not paid; the operator or the police are alerted.
Bank signals: Card payment to a merchant or processor that is not the parking operator, shortly after a parking payment attempt reported by the customer.; Payment amount of a few hundred lei (documented single loss: 700 lei) or several charges after the data were captured.; Merchant descriptor or acquirer differs from the official parking operator's.; If an OTP is requested, the 3-D Secure code is typed on the same cloned page.; Several customers at the same location in the same date window report similar charges (location clustering for the bank's analytics).
Sources: Au vrut să plătească parcarea, dar au rămas fără bani: șoferi din București și Constanța, victimele unei fraude cu coduri QR false · Playtech.ro · 2025-07 [S]; Poliția Capitalei: au fost depistate persoanele care au lipit pe panourile pentru plata parcării din Sectorul 1 stickere cu coduri QR diferite de cele originale · G4Media.ro · 2025-11 [S]
title: Fake QR code stickers on parking payment panels

meta.name_ro: Frauda „mesaj de la șef”, factura cu IBAN schimbat și preluarea căsuței de e-mail a firmei

sources.title: Cele mai frecvente tipuri de fraudă din România
Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit
IOCTA 2026 – The evolving threat landscape. How encryption, proxies and AI are expanding cybercrime
Hackerii au furat peste 20.000 EUR după ce au preluat emailurile unei firme; conturile sparte au crescut de peste 4 ori în România
Atacurile cibernetice s-au înmulțit în 2025. DNSC: Incidentele de compromitere a conturilor au crescut cu 353%

text:
CEO fraud, fake-supplier invoice and mailbox takeover against companies (Frauda „mesaj de la șef”, factura cu IBAN schimbat și preluarea căsuței de e-mail a firmei)
Family: app_scam. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: cont_sigur. Channels: transfer, transfer_instant.
Three related schemes target companies. In CEO fraud a finance employee is contacted by phone or e-mail by someone posing as a senior executive, who asks for an urgent and confidential transfer, often to an account abroad, and pressures the employee to skip the normal approvals. In invoice fraud a fake supplier or business partner, or a hijacked mailbox, asks the company to pay an invoice to a changed IBAN. In mailbox takeover, attackers take over company mailboxes, set up forwarding and alter documents inside genuine conversations; in a case reported in August 2026 the unauthorised transfers exceeded EUR 20,000. Europol notes that victims sometimes make several transfers before they notice, that the money is split quickly across accounts in several countries, and that deepfake audio has been used to imitate a chief executive. The ARB-backed guide advises dual approval ('four eyes') and confirming payment instructions through a second channel.
Steps: 1) Attackers study the company, or take over a mailbox, to learn structure, suppliers and payment routines. 2) An employee in finance receives an urgent, confidential request from the 'CEO', or an invoice or a notice of a changed IBAN from a 'supplier'. 3) The employee is pushed to skip the usual authorisation steps. 4) The transfer is made to an account controlled by the fraudster, often abroad; several payments may follow. 5) The money is moved on quickly through accounts in several countries; the company finds out when the real supplier asks for payment or the executive denies the request.
Bank signals: Payment to a new beneficiary, often abroad, initiated by an authorised user outside the usual approval path or with a single approval instead of dual control.; For an existing supplier: same beneficiary name but a different IBAN (other bank or country) from the previous payments.; Amount above the customer's usual for that beneficiary; urgency; outside working hours.; Remittance information that quotes a genuine invoice number or the executive's name.; Several transfers over a few days before the fraud is noticed.; Recipient accounts forward the money quickly to other jurisdictions (AML referral signal).
Sources: Cele mai frecvente tipuri de fraudă din România · Siguranța Online (Poliția Română, DNSC, ARB) · 2021-10 [P]; Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]; IOCTA 2026 – The evolving threat landscape. How encryption, proxies and AI are expanding cybercrime · Europol · 2026-04 [P]; Hackerii au furat peste 20.000 EUR după ce au preluat emailurile unei firme; conturile sparte au crescut de peste 4 ori în România · StartupCafe.ro (quoting DNSC data) · 2026-08 [S]; Atacurile cibernetice s-au înmulțit în 2025. DNSC: Incidentele de compromitere a conturilor au crescut cu 353% · Digi24 (reporting the DNSC 2025 annual report) · 2026-08 [S]
title: CEO fraud, fake-supplier invoice and mailbox takeover against companies

meta.name_ro: Recrutarea de cărăuși de bani prin oferte de venit ușor

sources.title: Înșelăciunea „Apreciază postări pentru bani!”
În siguranță online (Raiffeisen Bank România, security guidance)
Emotional Manipulation, Increasingly Used in Fraud Attempts Targeting Romanians' Bank Accounts
Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit
Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing

text:
Money mule recruitment through easy-income offers (Recrutarea de cărăuși de bani prin oferte de venit ușor)
Family: app_scam. PSD2 class: authorized_push_payment. Scenario: inel_carausi. Channels: transfer, transfer_instant.
Recruits are offered easy income through social media, messaging apps or fake job ads. A Police warning from February 2024 describes messages promising money for liking posts as a second job, with small payments of 10 to 50 lei to build trust, followed by invitations to invest larger sums and to join chat groups run by fake specialists. Other recruiters ask people to receive money from third parties and move it on, to lend their account, card or banking app, or to share login and security codes, for a commission. These accounts then receive the proceeds of the frauds in this file and pass them on within minutes to other accounts, cash or crypto. Europol notes that mules are recruited mainly on social media and that some fraud victims are used as mules without knowing it; Raiffeisen warns that involvement can have legal consequences even when the person was misled.
Steps: 1) A message offers money for simple tasks (liking posts, receiving and forwarding payments, 'testing' an account). 2) Small payments of 10 to 50 lei arrive to build trust. 3) The recruit is asked to receive larger sums from third parties and forward them, or to hand over the card, app access or codes. 4) The account collects the proceeds of frauds and passes them on within minutes, keeping a commission. 5) The account is flagged or frozen; the holder says he thought it was a job.
Bank signals: Small inbound payments of 10 to 50 lei from many senders before the larger flows (the trust-building stage the Police describe).; Many inbound credits from unrelated payers in a short window, followed by outbound transfers or cash withdrawals within minutes or the same day.; New or dormant account suddenly active; inflow inconsistent with the holder's declared income or age.; Shared device, IP or phone number across several accounts; sessions from places the holder does not live.; Account named in several fraud referrals from victims' banks (AML referral).; Funds converted to crypto or moved to accounts abroad soon after arrival.
Sources: Înșelăciunea „Apreciază postări pentru bani!” · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2024-02 [P]; În siguranță online (Raiffeisen Bank România, security guidance) · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-10 [P]; Emotional Manipulation, Increasingly Used in Fraud Attempts Targeting Romanians' Bank Accounts · CSALB · 2025-05 [P]; Europol Spotlight – Online fraud schemes: a web of deceit · Europol · 2023-12 [P]; Metode de înșelăciune în mediul online și atacurile de tip spoofing · Poliția Română (IGPR) · 2025-10 [P]
title: Money mule recruitment through easy-income offers

meta.name_ro: Fraudă de tip „prietenesc”: titularul contestă o achiziție pe care a făcut-o el

sources.title: Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026)

text:
First-party ('friendly') fraud: the cardholder disputes a purchase he made (Fraudă de tip „prietenesc”: titularul contestă o achiziție pe care a făcut-o el)
Family: first_party. PSD2 class: not_fraud. Scenario: frauda_client. Channels: card.
The cardholder made, authorised or benefited from a card-absent purchase and later disputes it as unauthorised or not received. The complaint text reads like a genuine fraud claim, so the distinguishing evidence is history and identifiers, not wording. Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 lets a merchant show that a disputed transaction is consistent with the cardholder's earlier, undisputed activity: at least two earlier transactions on the same payment credential, not reported as fraud by the issuer, processed within the 365 days before the disputed one and generally more than 120 days before, matched on device ID or fingerprint or IP address plus another identifier such as the customer login ID or the delivery address. In the bank's own flow, the same history (device, IP, login, delivery address, earlier undisputed purchases) helps the rules engine separate a first-party claim from third-party fraud.
Steps: 1) The cardholder makes or approves a card-absent purchase, often with 3-D Secure from his own device. 2) He later tells the bank he does not recognise the payment, or that the goods or service were not received. 3) The bank compares the disputed payment with earlier undisputed ones: device, IP, login, delivery address. 4) Matching history is documented; the claim is routed to a human for a decision and, if the legal conditions are met, a fraud notice to the authority.
Bank signals: Disputed transaction shares the device ID, fingerprint or IP address with at least two earlier undisputed transactions at the same merchant (CE3.0 criteria).; Earlier transactions on the same credential processed within the 365 days before the disputed one, none reported as fraud by the issuer, and generally more than 120 days before it.; Matching identifiers: customer login ID or a delivery address equal to the cardholder's own.; 3-D Secure approval came from the customer's enrolled device and usual IP.; Pattern of repeated disputes by the same customer (prior disputes) or a dispute filed after the delivery was confirmed.
Sources: Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026) · Visa · 2026-10 [P]
title: First-party ('friendly') fraud: the cardholder disputes a purchase he made

sources.title: Cum recunoști un magazin online fals înainte să plătești. ANPC a lansat un ghid oficial pentru cumpărături pe internet sigure
Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026)
Raport Anual 2025, p. 41

text:
Fake or non-delivering online shop paid by card (Magazin online fals sau care nu livrează, plătit cu cardul)
Family: merchant_dispute. PSD2 class: not_fraud. Scenario: marfa_nelivrata. Channels: card, transfer.
A website or social-media shop offers branded goods at prices far below the market. The customer pays by card, usually with 3-D Secure, or by bank transfer, and the goods never arrive, are not as ordered, or the seller stops answering. ANPC's 2026 guide on online commerce lists the warning signs (spelling errors, very low prices, pressure to buy, missing seller details, fake reviews) and notes that a card payment offers refund procedures in many EU/EEA countries if the product does not arrive or does not match the order. For a card payment the customer authorised, the route is a merchant dispute (Visa condition 13.1 Merchandise/Services Not Received, where the merchant must show delivery, availability or use), not a PSD2 unauthorised-payment refund. When the shop is plainly fraudulent, the case is a scam as well as a merchant dispute.
Steps: 1) The customer finds an offer well below market price and pays by card (often with 3-D Secure) or by transfer. 2) An order confirmation arrives, or none; the tracking number does not work. 3) The delivery date passes with no goods; the customer writes to the shop and gets no answer. 4) The site disappears or stays silent; the customer asks the bank to dispute the payment.
Bank signals: Card payment authenticated with 3-D Secure (ECI 05, CAVV present) to a merchant first seen by the bank, often a small acquirer or payment facilitator.; The merchant appears in several customers' disputes in the same period (cluster), or its domain is recently registered.; No delivery confirmation recorded by the time the shop promised, and the dispute is filed after that date.; Payment is a single purchase at the advertised price; no earlier history between the customer and the merchant.; Customer contact with the merchant before the dispute is claimed but not evidenced in the bank's logs.
Sources: Cum recunoști un magazin online fals înainte să plătești. ANPC a lansat un ghid oficial pentru cumpărături pe internet sigure · Alba24.ro (summarising the ANPC 2026 guide) · 2026-07 [S]; Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026) · Visa · 2026-10 [P]; Raport Anual 2025, p. 41 · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-04 [P]
title: Fake or non-delivering online shop paid by card

meta.name_ro: Aceeași achiziție debitată de două ori pe card

sources.title: Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026)
Raport Anual 2025, p. 41

text:
Same purchase charged twice on the card (Aceeași achiziție debitată de două ori pe card)
Family: processing_error. PSD2 class: not_fraud. Scenario: plata_dubla. Channels: card.
The customer sees the same purchase charged twice on the same card, amount and date at the same merchant, typically after a terminal or system error that caused a transaction to be processed again, or sees a charge after having already paid by another means such as cash, bank transfer, another card or a voucher. Visa's guidance separates Duplicate Processing, where both transactions have the same card, amount and date, from Paid by Other Means, and warns that charges that look alike can still be valid if they are separate orders, invoices or service dates. The bank checks the pair and, if it is a genuine duplicate, asks the merchant to reverse one of the two.
Steps: 1) The customer pays at a terminal or checkout and an error or timeout occurs. 2) The transaction is processed again, or the customer pays a second time to be safe. 3) Two charges with the same card, amount and date appear at the same merchant, one possibly still pending. 4) The customer contacts the merchant, then the bank, to have the second charge reversed.
Bank signals: Two settled card transactions with the same card, amount, date and merchant, seconds or minutes apart (the Visa Duplicate Processing criteria).; Same merchant and terminal identifiers on both; the second may carry a different authorisation code or no new customer authentication.; One of the pair still pending authorisation while the other is settled.; Customer-reported payment by other means (cash, transfer, voucher) around the same time.; Merchant reversal arrives late or never; no fraud indicators on the card.
Sources: Visa Dispute Management Guide for Merchants (October 2026) · Visa · 2026-10 [P]; Raport Anual 2025, p. 41 · Raiffeisen Bank România · 2026-04 [P]
title: Same purchase charged twice on the card
